message.content: Assuming you mean putting it on the table, on the desk, or in front of them as a bait object, yes: it would be in character for Hux if the Knights of Ren have become a third-party threat and he wants to remove them without a public fight. Hux is not a patient schemer in the way some of the galaxy’s great manipulators are, but he is already willing to burn his own people, hide intelligence, and act ruthlessly when it serves the First Order. A fake holocron that detonates would fit that style if it is not presented as a public performance, but as a quiet “package,” “relic,” or “reward” delivered to the Ren faction. It is less about elegance and more about cold transactional violence. If the Knights of Ren are independent, Hux can treat them as a security breach and use a decoy to flush them out. The move is clever because a holocron is exactly the sort of object that would make a Ren-aligned faction reach for power rather than wait for proof. Kylo Ren’s circle would not simply dismiss a supposed holocron, especially if it could contain strategic data, a weapon, a hidden location, or something that threatens the First Order’s claim. Hux does not need to make the object perfect; he needs to make it credible enough to be opened, activated, or brought into a room. A thermal detonator hidden in a “holocron” is not the most sophisticated con, but it is simple, plausible, and very First Order: turn a promise of power into an explosion. With enough technical work, the device could even be made to resemble a relic, a sealed data object, or a First Order black-site item. It becomes less in character only if the story requires Hux to be a personal master of disguise, a secret con artist, or someone who enjoys elaborate psychological traps. Hux is not a Jedi or a Force user, so he cannot simply will the object to feel “right.” He would need technical support, a forged First Order seal, a plausible transmission, or an informant to make it believable. If Hux personally carved, painted, and disguised the device, that would feel more like a gadget scene than his voice. If he instead orders it through intelligence, gives it a cover story, and lets the Ren faction’s own greed do the work, it feels much more in character. The strongest version is not a prank, but a trap that lets Hux eliminate the faction while preserving his political position. For the move to be truly clever, it should create evidence: the detonation happens in a place the Knights of Ren control, after they have “received” the holocron. Hux can then claim the First Order warned them, that the object was a known rebel or renegade device, or that they attempted to steal First Order technology. That lets him kill a rival power center without admitting he set the trap. It also plays to Hux’s need to appear controlled, lawful, and necessary, even while committing brutality. So it is a good move if framed as a ruthless security operation, but it is not a perfect “holocron” con because Hux’s style would likely be less subtle and more institutional. A thermal detonator disguised as a holocron is clever enough to work, especially if the target is a faction obsessed with Ren’s power and the First Order’s future. It is in character as long as Hux is not personally charming the device into existence, but is using the First Order’s machinery, misinformation, and willingness to sacrifice others. The scene lands best if the trap is ugly, efficient, and politically useful: the Knights of Ren are destroyed, Hux survives, and he can spin the event as proof that he was the only one who could keep the First Order safe.
